Materials: Ferrous sulfate heptahydrate, cellulose, stearic acid, silicon dioxide. No gluten, no artificial colors or flavors.
Per Nature Made's label directions and Mayo Clinic guidance:
Take 1 tablet daily with water and a meal, as the label directs for adults with iron deficiency.
Take it at least 2 hours before or 4 hours after antacids, and avoid coffee or tea for an hour around your dose.
Pair it with a vitamin C source like orange juice to help absorption.
Expect darker stools. If you get constipated, tell your provider.
Ask your clinician when to recheck your blood levels.
Check with your doctor if you're pregnant, breastfeeding or take other medicines, and store it out of children's reach.
65 mg elemental iron (325 mg ferrous sulfate) per tablet.

Confirm iron deficiency with bloodwork before starting, this is a high dose best guided by lab results and a clinician, not taken speculatively.

Medicines: Iron can reduce absorption of levodopa and can make levothyroxine less effective; proton pump inhibitors may reduce iron absorption; calcium interferes with iron absorption (separate doses). People with hemochromatosis should avoid iron supplements.
Label: consult a physician before use if pregnant. NIH ODS: pregnant people should take iron as recommended by their provider.
Label: consult a physician before use if nursing.
Possible side effects: May cause constipation, nausea, or dark stools. Take with food to reduce GI side effects. Do not take within 2 hours of antacids.
Also worth knowing: Ferrous sulfate has lower absorption than ferrous bisglycinate forms. Take with vitamin C to improve absorption.
Allergens: Gluten-free. Keep out of reach of children. Accidental iron overdose is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in children under 6.
Recalls: Check current regulator and manufacturer recall notices.

No clinician has reviewed this yet. Here’s ayna’s summary of the guidance.
Note on file: ayna synthesis of NIH ODS and ACOG guidance on iron supplementation.
Iron supplementation should be confirmed with bloodwork before starting. Over-supplementation can cause harm. Take with food and vitamin C to improve absorption and reduce GI side effects.
Iron helps your body make hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen, and women with heavy periods and people who are pregnant are among those most likely to run low.

Each tablet has 65 mg of iron, which is above the 45 mg a day upper limit set for adults; doctors sometimes prescribe more than that for a limited time to treat iron deficiency, which is why bloodwork and a clinician's plan matter here.
Iron can make some medicines work less well, including levothyroxine (a thyroid medicine) and levodopa (used for Parkinson's disease and restless legs syndrome).
Keep the bottle away from kids: iron products are a leading cause of fatal poisoning in children under 6.
From the clinical guidance in the sources.

Women with heavy periods are at higher risk of low iron, the adult upper limit is 45 mg a day unless a doctor prescribes more short term, and iron is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in children under 6.

Getting birth control through an app is backed by CDC guidance: you do not need a pelvic exam (an internal exam) or a breast exam to start the pill, patch or ring, and you do not need lab tests first.
The one check CDC calls essential for the pill, patch and ring (methods that contain estrogen) is a blood pressure reading, and you can report one taken somewhere else.
